text: An officer made one attempt at personal service. If nobody answered, the paper went on the apartment door immediately, and the legal clock began.
The officer did not have to return in the evening, on another day, or when the tenant was more likely to be home.
provenance: The Court set this out plainly.

text: The statute and the servers' practice made no provision for even a second attempt at handing the notice to someone.
provenance: The Court set this out plainly.

text: The opinion said nobody was home in a good percentage of cases, though it gave no time of day for those visits.
provenance: The opinion does not say what time of day the process servers came.

text: Posting was not automatically unconstitutional. The Court said it can often be an appropriate and effective substitute when personal service is inconvenient.
provenance: None of which, on its own, makes posting unconstitutional.

text: But missing someone once hardly shows that a tenant abandoned an apartment or stopped caring about the proceeding.
That is why a paper placed on the door after one failed visit was only formal notice, not reliable notice here.
The constitutional problem was not the knock itself. It was treating that single unanswered knock as the end of the search.
